source.title: SAIL: Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretable Alignment of Human Vision and Multimodal Large Language Models
source.authors: Tan-Guang Gao; Lu-Yuan Zhang; Yi-Fei Wang; Yun-Jia Wang; Hao-Tian Zhou; Mu-Fan Xue; Guo-Yuan Yang

record.tranche_reason: Applies SAE-based feature decomposition to multimodal large language models and reports feature-response redundancy and semantic-alignment results, providing indirect evidence in a new model setting rather than testing toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: Rows cover SAE-unit response-profile redundancy and semantic alignment between SAE-preferred images and voxel-preferred images. The paper also reports fLoc response reconstruction, cortical label maps, and action-related maps, but those outcomes do not directly measure the feature properties named in the claim versions. The study does not test overlapping directions, feature sparsity or importance effects, or feature recovery against known ground truth.
record.test_reason: The study uses SAEs as a tool to interpret alignment between MLLMs and fMRI voxels. Its results compare its own method (unified cross-layer SAE, SAIL) with a layer-wise SAE pipeline (SAEs-BrainMap) and with controls, on redundancy, semantic alignment, RSA and fLoc reconstruction. Superposition is cited as motivation (Elhage et al., 2022), but nothing tests whether MLLM features are superposed or spread across neurons. There is no neuron-level comparison and no recovery against known features. Nothing tests the completeness, stability, canonicality or dimensionality of SAE features. This fits T4: the study relies on the finding and reports its own method's performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also report that SAIL's semantic alignment beats single-unit, vision-tower and projector controls, and that this alignment is organized along the ventral visual pathway. They describe the action-semantics maps as exploratory. They make no claim about superposition itself.
record.recipe_differences: SAIL trains unified cross-layer sparse autoencoders on MLLM representations and aligns their units to human fMRI voxel responses; it does not reproduce the toy-network superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: Model architecture and evaluation mask are varied. The semantic-alignment comparison is stated in text for Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct; other-model comparisons are plotted without textual outcome descriptions.

fits_no_version.finding: SAEs trained independently per layer yield units with more duplicated response profiles across layers than a single SAE on concatenated layers (lower redundancy in all 4 models, 8 subjects, under 200 matched-size resamples).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Layer-wise SAE dictionaries contain cross-layer duplicate features, so per-layer SAE units are not a non-redundant set of model units.

record.problems: The study does not validate learned SAE features against ground-truth features or directly test superposition geometry. Redundancy results are described without numerical values, and semantic-alignment plots for three models do not have textual outcome descriptions in the supplied text. The analysis uses eight human subjects and a fixed natural-image stimulus set.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit. fLoc category reconstruction, cortical semantic maps, and action-semantic localization were not included because they report downstream brain-response or localization outcomes rather than directly testing the feature properties in the claim versions.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, no sparsity transition, no geometry.
All: no capacity or importance analysis.
No measure of features spread across neurons; no assessment of whether SAEs recover sparse features in the MLLMs beyond the study's use of them for brain alignment.
No test of completeness, stability across seeds or sizes, or canonicality.

record.verdict_notes: SAEs are applied to PCA-reduced, concatenated layer features with a 4x hidden dimension, so units are not even defined on the model's raw activation basis. All results are brain-alignment or method-comparison outcomes. The reader's 'tests/T3' and V4 'supports' labels are not justified.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity competition causes polysemanticity, or whether feature importance determines dedicated versus shared dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The paper studies SAE units in MLLMs, but does not establish feature recovery against ground truth, compare SAE features with neuron-level feature distributions, or directly show features spread across neurons.
Completeness, stability, and canonicality of SAE features as the model's units.
Whether model features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional structures.

rows.operation_detail: Compared maximum cosine similarity between held-out SAE-unit activation profiles for SAIL and SAEs-BrainMap.
rows.measure: Mean maximum cosine similarity of SAE-unit response profiles (redundancy)
rows.value: SAIL had lower redundancy distributions; exact value not stated
rows.uncertainty: 95% intervals shown for resampled differences; numerical bounds not stated
rows.note: The text reports higher redundancy for SAEs-BrainMap and positive SAEs-BrainMap-minus-SAIL differences for all eight subjects. Values are not given numerically.
rows.check: Compares redundancy between the study's own method (SAIL) and a competing SAE pipeline; this is a method comparison, not a measure of superposition or of SAE features as model units.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, semantic alignment averaged across eight subjects in Whole cortex and Selective ROI
reader_labels.reason: The text reports higher semantic alignment for SAIL than the layer-wise SAE comparator, alongside lower unit-response redundancy; this is indirect evidence that SAE units capture semantically relevant structure in an MLLM (R1, R5, R6).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, LLaVA-v1.6-Mistral-7B, LLaVA-v1.6-Vicuna-7B, and DeepSeek-VL-7B-Chat; eight subjects per model
reader_labels.reason: The text reports lower SAIL response-profile redundancy than SAEs-BrainMap for all tested subjects in all four models; this bears on the organization of SAE-derived features, but not on ground-truth feature recovery (R1–R4).
